cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(a): In 2012 the river States Norvalia, Pentra and Quessia concluded the Danara River Convention (DRC) on navigation on and protection of the Danara, which flows from Norvalia through Pentra into Quessia. Article 9 obliges each party to keep the navigation channel on its territory at least 2.5 m deep; Article 14 caps industrial discharges into the river. The DRC contains no clause on termination or withdrawal and is open to accession by any State. Under the DRC, signature expressed consent to be bound; for Norvalia it was signed by its Minister of Transport, who held full powers. In 2025 Norvalia's new government declares the DRC 'null and void' and stops complying with it. It argues (1) that during the negotiations Pentra's Prime Minister had promised the Minister of Transport a well-paid seat on the supervisory board of Pentra's state shipping company in return for his signature — a seat he took up after leaving office, which became public in 2014; and (2) that Norvalia's constitution requires parliamentary approval of treaties 'of major economic importance', which was never obtained. Until 2025 Norvalia had applied the DRC without objection and collected navigation fees under it. Assess Norvalia's arguments. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both arguments fail: corruption (Art 50 VCLT) is in principle a ground of invalidity, the constitutional violation was not manifest (Art 46), and Norvalia has in any case lost both grounds by acquiescing in the DRC for more than ten years (Art 45(b)).
• Corruption (Art 50): a State may invoke the corruption of its representative, directly or indirectly, by another negotiating State if it procured the State's consent — a substantial inducement, not a courtesy. A lucrative board seat promised by Pentra's Prime Minister for the signature qualifies, if proven.
• Internal law (Art 46): only a manifest violation — objectively evident to any State acting in accordance with normal practice and in good faith — of an internal rule of fundamental importance on competence to conclude treaties counts. Whether the DRC is 'of major economic importance' requires interpreting Norvalian law; the partners could rely on a minister with full powers (Art 7(1)(a)) and need not follow other States' constitutional law (Cameroon v Nigeria, ICJ 2002) → not manifest.
• Loss of the right (Art 45(b)): a State that, after becoming aware of the facts, acquiesced by its conduct in the treaty's validity can no longer invoke Arts 46–50. Norvalia knew of the missing approval since 2012 and of the board seat since 2014, yet applied the DRC and collected fees until 2025 → both grounds lost.
• Procedure: relative grounds make consent voidable, not void; Norvalia would have had to notify the parties in writing with reasons and, if they object, seek a peaceful settlement (Arts 65–67) — its unilateral non-performance breaches the DRC (Art 26). Even success would void only Norvalia's consent; the DRC would continue between Pentra and Quessia (Art 69(4)).
Memorise: Corruption (50) + manifest violation of a fundamental internal rule (46; Cameroon v Nigeria) = relative grounds → lost by acquiescence (45(b)) · procedure 65–67, not unilateral non-performance · only that State's consent falls (69(4)).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(b): In 2012 the river States Norvalia, Pentra and Quessia concluded the Danara River Convention (DRC) on navigation on and protection of the Danara, which flows from Norvalia through Pentra into Quessia. Article 9 obliges each party to keep the navigation channel on its territory at least 2.5 m deep; Article 14 caps industrial discharges into the river. The DRC contains no clause on termination or withdrawal and is open to accession by any State. In 2025 Norvalia's new government declared the DRC 'null and void' without following any procedure and stopped enforcing the Article 14 caps; since then Norvalian factories have discharged ten times the permitted quantity, causing massive fish deaths in Pentra's stretch of the river. Pentra wants to terminate the DRC in its relations with Norvalia; Quessia wants the DRC to remain in force among all parties. In addition, in 2025 an earthquake triggered a rockslide that blocks the navigation channel on Quessian territory; clearing it will take about three years, and Quessia announces that it will not perform its Article 9 obligation during that time. What rights do Pentra and Quessia have under the law of treaties? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Pentra, as a specially affected party, may only suspend the DRC in whole or in part in its relations with Norvalia (Art 60(2)(b) VCLT); termination towards Norvalia needs the unanimous agreement of all the other parties, which fails because Quessia refuses (Art 60(2)(a)). Quessia may only suspend its Article 9 obligation while the channel is blocked (Art 61(1)), not terminate.
• Material breach (Art 60(3)): a repudiation not sanctioned by the VCLT, or the violation of a provision essential to the object or purpose. Norvalia's 'null and void' declaration is a repudiation, and abandoning the discharge caps (tenfold excess) violates a core provision of a protection treaty → material breach.
• Multilateral treaty (Art 60(2)) — unlike under a bilateral treaty (Art 60(1)), the victim cannot terminate alone: (a) the other parties by unanimous agreement may suspend or terminate it towards the defaulter or among all; (b) a party specially affected by the breach may suspend it in whole or in part between itself and the defaulter — Pentra (fish deaths) qualifies and may e.g. suspend Norvalian ships' navigation rights on its stretch; (c) any party may suspend it only if the breach radically changes every party's position (integral treaties, e.g. disarmament) — not a river regime. Pentra may also invoke Norvalia's responsibility (cessation, reparation, countermeasures, Arts 49–54 ARSIWA).
• Quessia (Art 61): permanent disappearance or destruction of an object indispensable for execution → termination; temporary impossibility → only suspension; not if self-caused (Art 61(2)). An earthquake-induced rockslide blocking the channel for about three years → suspension of Art 9 for that period, limited to that clause if separable (Art 44(3)); in good faith Quessia must clear the channel as soon as feasible and not obstruct resumption (Arts 26, 72(2)). Under state responsibility the non-performance is also excused as force majeure (Art 23 ARSIWA).
• Both must follow Arts 65–67: written notification with reasons, a waiting period of at least three months (except in cases of special urgency), peaceful settlement if a party objects.
Memorise: material breach = repudiation or essential provision (60(3)) · multilateral: all others unanimously (60(2)(a)) · specially affected party only suspends (60(2)(b)) · integral treaty: any party suspends (60(2)(c)) · temporary impossibility → suspension only (61) · procedure 65–67.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(c): In 2012 the river States Norvalia, Pentra and Quessia concluded the Danara River Convention (DRC) on navigation on and protection of the Danara. Article 9 obliges each party to keep the navigation channel on its territory at least 2.5 m deep; Article 14 caps industrial discharges into the river; Article 16 obliges each party to designate riverside nature reserves. The DRC is open to accession by any State. In 2026 Austria, whose inland shipping companies use the Danara, wishes to accede to the DRC. Implementing Article 14 would require amendments to the federal Water Rights Act, and the designation of nature reserves is a matter within the autonomous competence of the Austrian Länder. Which steps does Austrian constitutional law (Article 50 B-VG) require for Austria to accede? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Approval by the Nationalrat (Art 50(1) Z 1 B-VG) and consent of the Bundesrat (Art 50(2) Z 2), then accession by the Federal President, deposit of the instrument and publication in the BGBl III (Art 49(2)).
• Nationalrat: implementing the DRC requires amending a federal law (Water Rights Act) → law-amending treaty → the Federal Government submits it and the Nationalrat must approve it (Art 50(1) Z 1); it may resolve that the DRC is to be fulfilled by enacting laws (Erfüllungsvorbehalt, Art 50(2) Z 4).
• Bundesrat: its consent is required insofar as the treaty regulates matters within the Länder's autonomous competence (nature reserves, Art 50(2) Z 2); otherwise it may only object as in legislation (Art 50(3) with Art 42(1)–(4)). The Länder must implement the DRC within their sphere (Art 16(4)).
• The Federal President concludes the treaty (Art 65(1)) on the Government's proposal and with countersignature (Art 67) → instrument of accession; its deposit establishes consent to be bound (Arts 15–16 VCLT). Then publication by the Federal Chancellor in the BGBl III (Art 49(2)).
Memorise: Govt bill → Nationalrat approval (50(1) Z 1) → Bundesrat consent for Länder matters (50(2) Z 2) / objection (50(3)) → [Erfüllungsvorbehalt 50(2) Z 4] → Federal President + countersignature (65, 67) → deposit → BGBl III (49(2)).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 1(d): The Danara River Convention (DRC), concluded in 2012 by Norvalia, Pentra and Quessia, caps industrial discharges into the Danara river in its Article 14 and is open to accession by any State. Austria, which must amend its federal Water Rights Act to implement Article 14, accedes to the DRC in 2026 after completing its domestic approval procedure under Article 50 B-VG. Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. 'As soon as the DRC has entered into force for Austria under international law, Austrian courts and authorities must apply Article 14 directly.' (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — international entry into force and domestic applicability are separate questions.
• Domestically the DRC applies only after the Federal Chancellor has published it in the BGBl III (Art 49(2) B-VG), and not directly if the Nationalrat adopted an Erfüllungsvorbehalt (Art 50(2) Z 4): then courts and authorities apply only the implementing laws. In any case only self-executing provisions can be applied directly.
• Internationally Austria is bound regardless and cannot invoke missing implementation (Art 27 VCLT).
Memorise: international EIF ≠ domestic applicability · BGBl III (49(2)) · Erfüllungsvorbehalt (50(2) Z 4) → implementing laws · Art 27 VCLT.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 2(a): Sofia, who holds only the nationality of State Arventa and lives there, trades in solar panels as a sole trader and stores her stock in a warehouse she rents in neighbouring State Brekonia. In March 2024 Brekonian police raided the warehouse, seized her entire stock without any compensation, stating that it was 'needed for the national energy transition', and detained Sofia for three weeks without bringing her before a judge. Sofia immediately sued Brekonia before its competent administrative court for the return of the stock and compensation for the detention; the court has scheduled the first hearing for 2031. Sofia asks the Arventan Foreign Ministry for help against Brekonia. What kind of help can Arventa give her under international law, and are its prerequisites met? (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Arventa can exercise diplomatic protection, i.e. invoke Brekonia's responsibility for the injury to its national; the prerequisites are met — wrongful acts of Brekonia, Sofia's continuous Arventan nationality, and local remedies need not be exhausted because of undue delay (Art 15(b) DADP) — but whether to act is for Arventa to decide.
• Concept (Art 1 ILC Draft Articles on Diplomatic Protection 2006, DADP): the invocation by a State, through diplomatic action or other means of peaceful settlement, of another State's responsibility for an injury caused by an internationally wrongful act to its national; the State asserts its own right (Mavrommatis, PCIJ 1924). Means: protest, negotiation, arbitration, the ICJ if jurisdiction exists — never force. Distinguish consular assistance (Arts 5, 36 VCCR, e.g. prison visits, finding a lawyer): no such conditions, but no claim against Brekonia.
• (1) Wrongful acts: the police are a State organ (Art 4 ARSIWA). Taking an alien's property without compensation violates the international minimum standard — even an expropriation for a public purpose requires compensation; three weeks' detention without judicial control is arbitrary (custom; Art 9 ICCPR if Brekonia is a party).
• (2) Nationality (Arts 3–5 DADP): Sofia is solely Arventan and lives there, from the date of injury to the presentation of the claim → continuous nationality; no dual-nationality or genuine-link problem.
• (3) Local remedies (Art 14 DADP; Interhandel 1959): normally all available remedies must be used first. Sofia sued at once, but a first hearing seven years later is undue delay attributable to Brekonia (Art 15(b)) → exhaustion is dispensed with.
• (4) Espousal: Arventa alone decides whether and how far to act (Barcelona Traction 1970). Aim: cessation and full reparation — return of the stock or compensation, compensation for the detention (Arts 30–37 ARSIWA).
Memorise: DP = the State's own right (Art 1 DADP, Mavrommatis) · wrongful act + continuous nationality (Art 5) + local remedies (Art 14; undue delay 15(b)) + discretion (Barcelona Traction) · ≠ consular assistance (Art 5 VCCR).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 2(b): Sofia, who holds only the nationality of State Arventa and lives there, stores her stock of solar panels in a warehouse she rents in neighbouring State Brekonia. In March 2024 Brekonian police seized her entire stock without any compensation and detained her for three weeks without bringing her before a judge. Her action before Brekonia's competent administrative court, filed immediately, has been scheduled for a first hearing only in 2031. Sofia asks Arventa for help, but its Foreign Ministry hesitates because it does not want to endanger a gas deal with Brekonia. Do you agree with the following statements? Give reasons. (1) 'Since Sofia fulfils all the conditions, Arventa is obliged under international law to take up her claim.' (2) 'Had Sofia accepted a clause in her Brekonian storage licence by which she waived the diplomatic protection of her home State and agreed to bring all disputes only before Brekonian courts, Arventa could no longer protect her.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Both statements are wrong: diplomatic protection is a discretionary right of Arventa, not a duty owed to Sofia; and Sofia cannot waive a right that belongs to her State — such a Calvo clause at most reinforces the local remedies rule.
• (1) The State is the sole judge whether, to what extent and for how long it grants protection, and may decide on political grounds such as a gas deal (Barcelona Traction, ICJ 1970). Art 19 DADP only recommends ('should') giving due consideration to protection; at most domestic constitutional law may give Sofia a right to have her request duly considered.
• (2) The right of protection is Arventa's own (Mavrommatis), so an individual cannot waive it. The clause binds Sofia to use Brekonian courts first (North American Dredging, US–Mexico General Claims Commission 1926), but it cannot exclude protection against an internationally wrongful act such as a denial of justice — and a first hearing only in 2031 is undue delay (Art 15(b) DADP).
Memorise: DP = the State's discretion (Barcelona Traction; Art 19 DADP only soft) · Calvo clause: no waiver of the State's right (Mavrommatis) → only reinforces local remedies (North American Dredging 1926).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 2(c): Sofia, a national of State Arventa, trades in solar panels and stores her stock in a warehouse she rents in neighbouring State Brekonia. In March 2024 Brekonian police raided the warehouse, seized her entire stock without any compensation and detained Sofia in Brekonia for three weeks without bringing her before a judge. Sofia now sues Brekonia before the courts of Arventa, claiming (1) compensation for the seized stock and for her detention and (2) payment for 200 solar panels that Brekonia's embassy in Arventa ordered from her in 2023 for the embassy roof and never paid for. Brekonia invokes state immunity. Assess. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Brekonia is immune for claim (1), because police seizure and detention are sovereign acts (acta iure imperii) even if unlawful; it is not immune for claim (2), because ordering solar panels is by its nature a commercial transaction (actum iure gestionis).
• Restrictive immunity (par in parem non habet imperium; custom — Jurisdictional Immunities, Germany v Italy, ICJ 2012; UN Convention 2004, UNCSI, not in force but largely reflecting custom): primarily the nature of the act decides, its purpose only exceptionally (Art 2(2) UNCSI).
• (1) Police measures are classic imperium, and their illegality does not remove immunity (Germany v Italy). The tort exception (Art 12 UNCSI) requires an act in the forum State — these acts occurred in Brekonia. Sofia's route is diplomatic protection.
• (2) A purchase any private person could make → no immunity (Art 10 UNCSI); the embassy purpose does not make it sovereign (Empire of Iran, German BVerfG 1963 — repair of the embassy heating).
• Execution is a separate question: the embassy bank account serves the mission's functions and stays immune (Philippine Embassy, BVerfG 1977; Art 21(1)(a) UNCSI).
Memorise: jurisdiction = nature of the act (Art 2(2) UNCSI) · police = imperii, immune even if unlawful · tort exception only for acts in the forum (12) · purchase = gestionis (10, Empire of Iran) · enforcement separate (purpose of the asset).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 2(d): Sofia, a national of State Arventa, trades in solar panels in Arventa and in neighbouring State Brekonia. Brekonia's ambassador to Arventa, Mr Valen, a Brekonian national, owes her money: (1) he has not paid for solar panels she installed on his privately owned holiday house in Arventa; (2) alongside his post he runs a paid business as sales agent for Brekonian solar manufacturers in Arventa, and he owes Sofia a commission under a contract concluded in that business. Can Sofia sue Mr Valen before the courts of Arventa? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Not for claim (1) — the ambassador is immune from civil jurisdiction, and a payment claim is not a 'real action' relating to private immovable property; yes for claim (2), which relates to a commercial activity outside his official functions (Art 31(1)(c) VCDR).
• Art 31(1) VCDR: a diplomatic agent (not a national of the receiving State, so no Art 38 restriction) is immune from civil and administrative jurisdiction except for (a) real actions relating to private immovable property in the receiving State, (b) succession matters in which he is involved as a private person, (c) actions relating to professional or commercial activity outside his official functions.
• (1) A claim for the price is contractual, not about title to or possession of the house; contracts incidental to private daily life are not 'commercial activity' (Tabion v Mufti, US 1996) → immune.
• (2) A paid agency business for profit is commercial activity (forbidden to diplomats, Art 42) → no immunity; execution only without infringing his person or residence (Art 31(3)).
• For claim (1) remain: an express waiver by Brekonia (Art 32), a suit in Brekonia (Art 31(4)), or a suit once his functions have ended and he has left — immunity then covers only official acts (Art 39(2)).
Memorise: Art 31(1) exceptions: real action on private immovables · succession · commercial activity outside functions · payment claim ≠ real action · daily-life contracts ≠ commercial · waiver (32), home courts (31(4)), after office only official acts (39(2)).

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(a): States Corvania and Dalmor, both UN members, are parties to the ICCPR and to the 1984 Convention against Torture (CAT), without reservations. Corvania has made a declaration under Article 36(2) of the ICJ Statute; Dalmor has not. Credible reports show that opposition activists detained in Dalmor's prisons — all of them Dalmorian nationals — are systematically tortured by Dalmor's security service and by the 'Wardens', a militia that the security service arms, pays and directs in its operations. Corvania sent several diplomatic notes demanding an end to the torture and proposing negotiations; Dalmor did not reply. Corvania then formally requested arbitration under Article 30(1) CAT; seven months later the two States have still not agreed on the organisation of the arbitration. Corvania files an application against Dalmor before the ICJ. Does the ICJ have jurisdiction, and may Corvania bring the case although none of the victims is its national? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Yes: the optional clause does not help because Dalmor has made no declaration, but the compromissory clause of Art 30(1) CAT applies and its preconditions are met; Corvania has standing because the CAT obligations are owed erga omnes partes (Belgium v Senegal, ICJ 2012).
• Consent: only States may be parties (Art 34 ICJ Statute; as UN members both are parties to the Statute, Art 93(1) Charter), and the Court needs their consent. Art 36(2) operates only between States that have both accepted it (reciprocity) → no basis. A compromissory clause covers 'matters specially provided for in treaties and conventions in force' (Art 36(1)).
• Art 30(1) CAT: a dispute on the interpretation or application of the CAT that cannot be settled by negotiation goes to arbitration at one party's request; if within six months the parties cannot agree on its organisation, either may refer it to the ICJ. Here a dispute exists (Corvania's claims met Dalmor's silence where a reply was called for), Corvania genuinely tried to negotiate, requested arbitration, and seven months have passed → met. The Court decides on its own jurisdiction (Art 36(6)).
• Standing: not diplomatic protection — the victims are Dalmor's own nationals. But all CAT parties share a common interest in compliance, so any party may invoke another party's responsibility (Belgium v Senegal paras 68–70; Art 48(1)(a) ARSIWA; likewise The Gambia v Myanmar 2022 under the Genocide Convention).
Memorise: only States + consent · Art 36(2) needs both declarations · Art 30(1) CAT: negotiation fails → arbitration request → 6 months → ICJ · erga omnes partes standing (Belgium v Senegal 2012; Art 48 ARSIWA) ≠ diplomatic protection.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(b): States Corvania and Dalmor are parties to the ICCPR and to the Convention against Torture (CAT), without reservations. Corvania has brought a case against Dalmor before the ICJ on the basis of Article 30(1) CAT, alleging that opposition activists detained in Dalmor's prisons — all of them Dalmorian nationals — are systematically tortured by Dalmor's security service and by a militia it arms, pays and directs. While the case is pending, Corvania learns that the torture continues and that Dalmor is destroying prison records. It asks the Court to act urgently. Under what conditions may the ICJ indicate provisional measures, and would they bind Dalmor? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The ICJ may indicate provisional measures (Art 41 ICJ Statute) if it has prima facie jurisdiction, the rights claimed are plausible and linked to the measures requested, and there is a real and imminent risk of irreparable prejudice (urgency); the measures are binding.
• Application: prima facie jurisdiction under Art 30(1) CAT; the right of the detainees not to be tortured and Corvania's right to compliance are plausible; continuing torture threatens life and health, and the destruction of records threatens the evidence → irreparable and urgent. The Court may also indicate measures other than those requested (Art 75(2) Rules of Court).
• Precedent: Canada and the Netherlands v Syria (Order of 16 November 2023) — Syria was ordered to prevent torture, also by persons under its control, direction or influence, and to preserve evidence.
• Binding force: LaGrand (ICJ 2001) — provisional measures are binding; non-compliance is a separate breach.
Memorise: Art 41 Statute: prima facie jurisdiction + plausible rights + link + irreparable prejudice/urgency · binding (LaGrand 2001) · Syria 2023: prevent torture, preserve evidence.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(c): States Corvania and Dalmor are parties to the ICCPR and to the Convention against Torture (CAT), without reservations. Credible reports show that opposition activists detained in Dalmor's prisons — all of them Dalmorian nationals — are systematically tortured by Dalmor's security service and by the 'Wardens', a militia that the security service arms, pays and directs in its operations. Corvania has brought a case against Dalmor before the ICJ under Article 30(1) CAT. Before the Court, Dalmor argues: (1) the detainees are its own nationals, so their treatment is a purely internal affair; (2) most acts of torture were committed by the Wardens, a private militia, not by State organs; (3) because of a terrorist threat it has proclaimed a state of emergency and derogated from the ICCPR, so the prohibition of torture is suspended. Do you agree with Dalmor? Give reasons. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No to all three: human rights bind a State towards everyone within its jurisdiction, including its own nationals; Dalmor answers for the Wardens' torture (Art 8 ARSIWA if its security service controls their operations, and in any case through official acquiescence and its own duty to prevent); and the prohibition of torture is non-derogable and ius cogens.
• (1) Since the UN Charter (Arts 1(3), 55(c), 56) human rights are a matter of international law and belong to individuals regardless of nationality (unlike diplomatic protection); the ICCPR covers 'all individuals within its territory and subject to its jurisdiction' (Art 2(1)), the CAT 'any territory under its jurisdiction' (Art 2(1) CAT). Matters governed by treaties a State has accepted are no longer purely domestic (Nationality Decrees, PCIJ 1923: a relative question); Art 2(7) Charter only limits the UN.
• (2) Private conduct is attributable if done on the State's instructions or under its direction or control (Art 8 ARSIWA) — effective control over the specific operations (Nicaragua 1986; Bosnian Genocide 2007). Arming and paying alone do not suffice; if the security service directs the operations in which detainees are tortured, Art 8 is met. Either way, torture in Dalmor's own prisons occurs at least with the 'consent or acquiescence' of public officials (Art 1 CAT), and Dalmor breaches its own duty to prevent, investigate and punish (Arts 2(1), 12 CAT; Art 2(1) ICCPR 'respect and ensure').
• (3) Art 4(2) ICCPR makes Art 7 (torture) non-derogable; the CAT has no derogation clause — 'no exceptional circumstances whatsoever' justify torture (Art 2(2) CAT); the prohibition is ius cogens (Belgium v Senegal 2012, para 99).
Memorise: HR bind towards own nationals too (Charter 1(3), 55–56; ICCPR 2(1)) · militia: Art 8 ARSIWA only with effective control (Nicaragua, Bosnian Genocide); CAT Art 1 'acquiescence'; duty to prevent · torture non-derogable (Art 4(2) ICCPR, Art 2(2) CAT), ius cogens.

cards.q: Mock exam 3 — Question 3(d): States Corvania and Dalmor, both UN members, are parties to the Convention against Torture (CAT). Corvania, none of whose nationals is affected, brought a case against Dalmor before the ICJ under Article 30(1) CAT concerning the systematic torture of detained Dalmorian opposition activists. In its final judgment the ICJ finds that Dalmor has violated the CAT and orders it to end the torture and to submit the cases to its competent authorities for the purpose of prosecution. Dalmor ignores the judgment, calling it a 'mere recommendation'. What can Corvania do? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Dalmor is wrong — the judgment is binding and final; Corvania may turn to the Security Council (Art 94(2) UN Charter) and use retorsion, while countermeasures by a State that is not itself injured are contested.
• Binding force: the decision binds the parties in respect of that case (Art 59 ICJ Statute), is final and without appeal (Art 60), and every UN member undertakes to comply (Art 94(1) Charter) → non-compliance is a new wrongful act.
• Security Council: may, if it deems necessary, make recommendations or decide upon measures to give effect to the judgment (Art 94(2)) — subject to the veto of the permanent members (the US vetoed such a draft after Nicaragua 1986).
• Own reactions: retorsion (lawful unfriendly acts, e.g. downgrading relations, stopping aid) is always possible. Countermeasures (Arts 49–54 ARSIWA) clearly belong to injured States; Corvania invokes responsibility under Art 48, and Art 54 only reserves 'lawful measures' → its right to countermeasures is contested. Never force (Art 2(4) Charter). Political pressure: General Assembly, Human Rights Council.
Memorise: Arts 59, 60 Statute + Art 94(1) Charter = binding, final · Art 94(2) Security Council (veto) · retorsion yes · countermeasures by a non-injured State contested (Arts 48, 54 ARSIWA) · no force.
